People have got the rule differences and design approaches nailed down pretty well, so I'm going to explain the difference between the themes of the various supernatural games.

**Vampire**

Masquerade: This game aimed to be a personal horror experience but quickly transformed into an action game due to the constant and often violent conflict between two factions. While you play as a creature with potentially endless life, the end of the world is rapidly approaching and you are running out of time.

Requiem: This game actually achieved the personal horror that was originally intended. The two factions have been replaced with five groups that are less openly hostile to each other, allowing for more nuanced political maneuvering. Vampires have unreliable memories and there is no agreed-upon origin for them. The major antagonists are a race of shadowy, owl-like creatures that claim a distant ancestry with vampires and detest humanity.

**Werewolf**

Apocalypse: The end of the world is coming and chances are good that it's too late to do anything to stop it. Werewolves are warriors created by a primal force to be her defenders, and they are here to stop a destructive entity from annihilating all existence. Werewolves are divided into 13 different tribes who can barely cooperate together at the best of times. The themes often center around environmental issues and misanthropy with a healthy dose of existential nihilism.

Forsaken: Werewolves are created by the union of two spirits in prehistoric times: a lunar spirit and a primal predator. Eventually, the predator grew sick and old, leading some werewolves to decide he needed to be put down. Those who killed him became Forsaken, burdened with the responsibility of policing the boundaries between the physical world and the spirit realm for all time. Those who did not are Pure, cursed for a crime they didn't commit and dedicated to the destruction of the Forsaken. In this game, werewolves are the ultimate hunters rather than warriors, focusing more on the pack than on larger global conflicts, and everything is painted in shades of grey rather than an obvious good versus evil narrative.

**Mage**

Ascension: Reality is not fixed, but based on the consensus of mankind's collective unconsciousness. A few individuals are able to awaken to this fact and can shape reality to suit their own desires, but if the unaware see acts of magic that violate their understanding of the world, the mage suffers from Paradox. The mystically focused Council of Traditions and the science-focused Technocracy are locked in a centuries-long battle to determine the nature of reality.

Awakening: The world has fallen due to human hubris. The reality we perceive is a pale shadow of a much grander existence that is cut off from us by a reality-destroying chasm. Only five watchtowers in the higher realms can cut through this chasm and call out to the souls of certain individuals, who become mages. Mages are driven by their knowledge to uncover mysteries and search for symbols of the higher realms in the fallen world. Paradox occurs when mages draw on more power than they can handle and attract the attention of the chasm.

**Ghosts**

Oblivion: You're dead and because of your angst, unfinished business, and refusal to accept death, you failed to pass on to the true afterlife and are stuck in a purgatory. Additionally, you have an evil voice inside your head that will tempt you into giving it more and more power so it can turn you into a servant of the reality-destroying maelstrom. Welcome to the bleakest, most depressing game ever made.

Sin-Eaters: You almost died, but at the brink of the afterlife, a strange ghost/spirit hybrid made a deal with you: it can bring you back to life, make you stronger, even give you supernatural powers, but in return, it gets to ride along inside your head and body. So it's great, you got a second chance at life, feeling better than ever, except you can see ghosts now, and they want you to help them resolve their issues so they can pass on as well. Also, that new voice inside you is kind of weird and doesn't quite understand humanity or morality.

**Changeling**

Dreaming: So faeries used to be real and they had a whole world of their own, but it's gone now along with the faeries, except for fragments of the souls of a few faeries who constantly get reincarnated into human bodies. You are part human, part fae, and you need to keep imagination alive in an increasingly cynical and nihilistic world that no longer believes in magic or dreams.

The Lost: You were once an ordinary person until one of the all-powerful fae abducted you and held you as a slave in their nightmare realm. You managed to escape, but your time in that realm has permanently changed you into a fae creature. Now you need to reclaim your old life or build a new one while trying to hide from your former captors.

For starters we would have to ask ourselves: what is this game about? Well from my reading it's about being a cursed monster who has to feed off humanity to slake unnatural hungers while being in turn hunted by the few humans who are aware that you exist. This sounds familiar because as a concept it was already executed to great commercial and critical success by another game in the early 90s. Okay so this game isn't treading fresh ground but the problem like I said before is that it is in denial about its own nature and it pretends that it's something like another game where sure we might be monsters, but we're good monsters trying to make the world better. Except in those games you're either trying to save the world from the apocalypse or you're trying to protect the world from amoral predatory spirits. One of those games gets to turn what would otherwise be slavering monstrosities into compelling protagonists by successfully making the case that they are necessary and despite their nastier elements, they do make the world a better place. This game falls at this hurdle, I don't get the sense that its "teaching a lesson" angle of what they do is anything other than a flimsy, post-hoc rationalization for being monsters and that sucks. Frankly their methods are terrible, all they can do is instill avoidance behavior and there's no guarantee their victims might even understand there's a lesson there at all. Other monsters don't go around telling themselves that their actions are for the victims' own good, they do it because they are monsters and humans are their prey. Both games acknowledge that these monsters are not nice beings, and the ones who try to be are struggling hard against that nature.

So like I said the first step is to drop the "lessons" bit, or keep it but present it as a weak excuse that those uncomfortable with their nature use to deny what they really have become. The rules on feeding don't support it anyway, a powerful monster can amass a horrific reputation as a terrifying being who collects trophies and the only lesson he would need to teach is "don't be outside when the guy with the mask comes to harvest." So with that angle gone, this game is sort of stuck getting too close to the other game's territory, it's a game of personal horror where the horror comes from facing what you are and what you have to do to keep worse things from happening. Its selling point is that while the other game pigeonholes you into being a specific type of monster, this game allows for a broader range of possibilities.

The other major issue that needs to be addressed is the heroes. They're a mess and we all know it and I don't need to explain why. So let's just make them more sympathetic, since sympathetic villains are a sign of a good writer. The first step to fixing them is acknowledging that heroes are the result of monsters failing at being good monsters (a good monster is not a "teacher of wisdom" but one who keeps their darker urges in check and is not too proud of some of the things they have to do as a result). Heroes are born from monsters screwing up and letting their darker sides ruin another person. A monster should confront a hero with a mixture of shame and disappointment, not scorn and ridicule. Also, heroes should not be universally unlikable; they can be obsessed, monomaniacal, and self-involved, but they do have a point: monsters are real and they ruined my life. They turned me into an emotional wreck and I want, no need, payback. When I first read about heroes when this game was being pitched I thought about a character from a popular series. Yes, that character was a selfish, narcissistic little brat who nearly caused disaster, but he was also a product of the protagonists screwing up and inflicting their nightmare life onto a scared kid who wasn't mentally or emotionally prepared for it. That character was still one of the biggest threats the protagonists ever faced, but the tragedy of his situation is what made his story stick with me for over 20 years. So that's my take on it. Oh also that rule about how monsters get a bonus and an automatic advantage when dealing with other supernatural beings can go right off and be disregarded.

How to Fix This Game TL;DR: drop the "we're doing it for your own good" attitude, make monsters sympathetic by making them afraid of their own darker sides and what those sides can do if unchecked, and make heroes less one-dimensional and more complex.
